uncited: *   Input geometry: A set of 2D primitives (e.g., triangles) defined in 3D space.
*   Voxel grid resolution: $N_x, N_y, N_z$ (number of voxels along each axis).
*   Grid bounds: $P_{min}$ and $P_{max}$ defining the world-space extent of the voxel grid.
*   A set of occupied voxel indices $S_d \subset \mathbb{Z}^3$.
*   **Voxel Grid**: A 3D boolean array or bitfield of size $N_x \times N_y \times N_z$.
*   **Depth Buffer**: A 2D buffer for each of the three passes, storing the depth value of the rasterized primitive at each pixel center.
**Initialize** the voxel grid $S_d$ to empty.
**Setup Projection**: Configure the camera or projection matrix such that the view direction is aligned with axis $A$.
For example, for the Z-pass, the camera looks down the Z-axis.
**Rasterize**: Render the input primitives to a 2D screen space corresponding to the other two axes (e.g., X-Y plane for the Z-pass).
**Evaluate Depth**: For each pixel $(u, v)$ in the screen space that is covered by the rasterization, retrieve the depth value $d_{prim}$ of the primitive at the pixel center.
**Map to Voxel**: Calculate the voxel index $(i, j, k)$ corresponding to the pixel center.
The index along the projection axis $A$ is determined by the depth $d_{prim}$.
Specifically, find the voxel whose center is closest in depth to $d_{prim}$.
**Mark Voxel**: Set the voxel at $(i, j, k)$ in $S_d$ to occupied.
For a pass along axis $A$, let the screen coordinates be $(u, v)$ corresponding to spatial coordinates $(x, y)$ or $(y, z)$ or $(z, x)$.
The depth $d_{prim}(u, v)$ is the value of the primitive at the center of the pixel.
The other two indices $k_B, k_C$ are derived directly from the pixel coordinates $(u, v)$ mapped to the grid bounds.
*   **Precision**: Standard floating-point depth buffers are sufficient, but care must be taken with z-fighting if primitives are coplanar with the projection direction.

*   **Time Complexity**: $O(N_{prim} \cdot N_{screen})$ per pass, where $N_{prim}$ is the number of primitives and $N_{screen}$ is the number of pixels in the screen space (approximately $N_x N_y + N_y N_z + N_z N_x$).
*   **Memory Complexity**: $O(N_x N_y N_z)$ for the voxel grid, plus $O(N_{screen})$ for the depth buffers.
It is generally faster than ray-marching based voxelization for complex scenes.
*   **Strengths**: Produces minimal 6-separating voxelization; simple to implement using standard graphics APIs; handles curved primitives well.
*   **Limitations**: Requires three passes; may produce artifacts if the depth evaluation is not accurate (e.g., z-fighting); not suitable for 26-connected ray marching without additional processing.
It is equivalent to the GPU-based voxelization methods used by Forest et al. [FBP09] and Crassin et al. [CNS*11].
The theoretical basis for 6-separating voxelization using crosshairs intersection targets was established by Cohen-Or and Kaufman [COK97] and further developed in subsequent works.
